title: Preparing for a new dog
steps: Set up a quiet sleeping place, fresh water, suitable food, a collar or harness and secure identification.
Arrange a vet appointment, discuss vaccinations and parasite prevention, and plan gradual introductions.
caution: Allow time to settle; avoid overwhelming the dog with visitors.

title: Choosing suitable equipment
steps: Select a comfortable well-fitting harness or collar, lead, bowls, bed and safe chew toys.
Check fit regularly, particularly for growing puppies; inspect toys for wear.
caution: Avoid equipment that restricts breathing or causes pain.

title: Dog identification and microchipping
steps: Make sure your dog is microchipped and your keeper details are up to date.
Use a collar identification tag when out, as required by local law.
caution: In the UK dogs must be microchipped and registered on a compliant database; check current rules.

title: Creating a calm daily routine
steps: Keep meals, toilet breaks, rest, walks and play reasonably predictable.
Build in quiet time and adjust the routine for age, health and individual needs.
caution: Avoid rigid routines that prevent necessary toilet breaks or rest.

title: Introducing a dog to a new home
steps: Start with one or two quiet rooms and show the dog where water and resting places are.
Let the dog explore at its own pace and reward calm behaviour.
caution: Never force contact or punish fearful behaviour.

title: Choosing a complete dog food
steps: Choose a nutritionally complete food appropriate to your dog's life stage and needs.
Follow the maker's feeding guide as a starting point and monitor body condition.
caution: Ask your vet about therapeutic diets or significant dietary changes.

title: Changing food gradually
steps: Mix a small amount of the new food with the usual food and increase gradually over about a week.
Watch appetite, stool and comfort during the change.
caution: Seek veterinary advice for persistent vomiting, diarrhoea or refusal to eat.

title: Fresh drinking water
steps: Provide clean fresh water at all times and wash bowls regularly.
Take water on walks and in hot weather; check intake changes.
caution: Sudden excessive thirst or inability to drink warrants veterinary advice.

title: Safe treat habits
steps: Use small portions of dog-safe treats for training and enrichment.
Count treats within the daily food allowance and choose size-appropriate chews.
caution: Avoid grapes, raisins, chocolate, xylitol and cooked bones; ask a vet about any ingestion.

title: Monitoring body condition
steps: Feel for ribs under a light covering of tissue and look for a visible waist from above.
Track weight periodically and discuss changes with your vet.
caution: Rapid unexplained weight change can indicate illness.

title: Foods to keep away from dogs
steps: Store chocolate, grapes, raisins, onions, garlic, alcohol and xylitol-containing products securely.
Keep bins closed and remind visitors not to offer table scraps.
caution: If your dog eats a potentially toxic item, contact a vet promptly; do not induce vomiting unless instructed.

title: Planning age-appropriate walks
steps: Choose walk length and pace based on breed, age, fitness and weather.
Let your dog sniff and take breaks; increase activity gradually.
caution: Avoid strenuous exercise for puppies or dogs with health conditions without veterinary advice.

title: Safe outdoor play
steps: Use a secure area and appropriate toys for fetch, searching and gentle games.
Check the ground for hazards and provide water and rest.
caution: Stop if the dog limps, overheats or appears exhausted.

title: Scent games at home
steps: Hide a few pieces of regular food in easy-to-find places or a snuffle mat.
Make searches gradually more challenging while supervising.
caution: Use only dog-safe items and prevent swallowing of fabric or toy parts.

title: Food puzzles and enrichment
steps: Try a suitable food puzzle or lick mat with part of the daily ration.
Supervise the first sessions and clean the equipment after use.
caution: Avoid puzzle pieces small enough to swallow.

title: Helping a bored dog
steps: Rotate safe toys, add sniffing opportunities and short reward-based training sessions.
Balance mental activity with sufficient sleep and calm downtime.
caution: Destructive behaviour may reflect anxiety or medical problems, not just boredom.

title: Reward-based basic training
steps: Reward the behaviour you want immediately with food, play or praise.
Practise short sessions for cues such as sit, come and wait.
caution: Avoid intimidation, punishment or aversive training tools.

title: Teaching a reliable recall
steps: Start indoors or in a secure area and reward every return enthusiastically.
Progress to a long training line in safe places before trying more distractions.
caution: Do not let a dog off lead where recall is unreliable or unsafe.

title: Loose-lead walking
steps: Reward your dog for staying near you when the lead is slack.
Pause or change direction gently when pulling begins; practise in quiet areas.
caution: Do not jerk the lead or use devices that cause pain.

title: Toilet training a puppy
steps: Take your puppy outside after waking, eating, play and at frequent intervals.
Reward toileting outdoors and clean indoor accidents without punishment.
caution: Sudden accidents in a previously trained dog may need a vet check.

title: Managing separation worries
steps: Practise very short, comfortable absences and return before distress builds.
Provide a safe resting area and seek a qualified behaviour professional for persistent distress.
caution: Do not use punishment or leave a panicking dog to cry it out.

title: Understanding dog body language
steps: Watch posture, tail, ears, eyes, movement and the overall context.
Give space when a dog freezes, turns away, lip-licks repeatedly or growls.
caution: A wagging tail alone does not always mean a dog is comfortable.

title: Introducing dogs safely
steps: Start with distance in a neutral outdoor space and reward calm behaviour.
Keep leads loose, allow breaks and separate if either dog becomes tense.
caution: Do not force face-to-face greetings or ignore signs of fear.

title: Brushing the coat
steps: Use a brush appropriate to coat type and work gently in short sessions.
Check for mats, skin irritation, fleas and debris while grooming.
caution: Never cut tight mats close to the skin with scissors.

title: Bathing your dog
steps: Use lukewarm water and dog-formulated shampoo only when needed.
Rinse thoroughly and dry carefully, especially skin folds and ears.
caution: Avoid getting shampoo in eyes and ears; ask a vet about irritated skin.

title: Checking paws after walks
steps: Inspect pads and between toes for stones, grass seeds, cuts or irritation.
Rinse off road salt or other residues and dry the paws.
caution: Deep cuts, swelling or persistent licking need veterinary assessment.

title: Nail care basics
steps: Check whether nails are overlong or clicking heavily on hard floors.
Ask a groomer or vet to demonstrate safe trimming if unsure.
caution: Cutting the quick is painful and can bleed; do not force handling.

title: Cleaning food and water bowls
steps: Wash bowls with warm water and suitable washing-up liquid, then rinse well.
Clean more frequently when using wet food or in hot weather.
caution: Avoid leaving cleaning-product residue on bowls.

title: Looking after ears
steps: Check for unusual smell, redness, discharge or repeated head shaking.
Only clean ears with a vet-recommended product if advised.
caution: Do not insert cotton buds into the ear canal.

title: Dental care and toothbrushing
steps: Introduce dog-safe toothpaste and a soft dog toothbrush gradually with rewards.
Brush regularly as tolerated and ask your vet about dental checks.
caution: Never use human toothpaste, which may contain harmful ingredients.

title: Routine veterinary check-ups
steps: Arrange regular veterinary health checks and discuss weight, teeth and mobility.
Keep a record of medications, vaccination history and any changes in behaviour.
caution: Online guides cannot diagnose illness.

title: Vaccinations and boosters
steps: Ask your vet which core and lifestyle-related vaccinations your dog needs.
Record dates and discuss the appropriate booster schedule with your practice.
caution: Vaccination schedules vary with the dog and local disease risks.

title: Flea and tick prevention
steps: Discuss an appropriate prevention plan with your vet or veterinary professional.
Check the coat after outdoor activities, particularly around ears and skin folds.
caution: Never use cat or dog parasite products interchangeably without veterinary advice.

title: Worming and parasite checks
steps: Ask your vet about a risk-based worming and testing plan.
Pick up faeces promptly and wash hands after handling waste.
caution: Do not guess medicine doses or use unlicensed remedies.

title: Recognising urgent warning signs
steps: Watch for breathing difficulty, collapse, repeated seizures, a swollen painful abdomen or severe bleeding.
Contact an emergency veterinary service immediately if these occur.
caution: Do not wait for an app checklist to confirm an emergency.

title: What to do if your dog may be poisoned
steps: Move the dog away from the suspected substance and keep packaging or a photo of it.
Call your vet or emergency vet promptly with the substance and estimated amount.
caution: Do not induce vomiting or give home remedies unless directed by a vet.

title: Keeping a health and medication record
steps: Note vet visits, prescribed medication, doses as labelled, allergies and follow-up dates.
Keep your vet's contact number and emergency details handy.
caution: Only give medicines prescribed or approved for that dog by a vet.

title: Keeping dogs safe in hot weather
steps: Walk in cooler hours, provide shade and plenty of water, and avoid hot pavement.
Watch for heavy panting, weakness, confusion or collapse.
caution: Suspected heatstroke is an emergency: begin safe cooling and contact a vet urgently.

title: Cold-weather dog care
steps: Adjust walk duration to coat, age and health; dry wet fur and paws after outings.
Offer a warm draught-free resting place and avoid frozen water hazards.
caution: Small, elderly and short-coated dogs may need extra protection.

title: Fireworks and loud noises
steps: Provide a safe den and close curtains before noisy events.
Allow your dog to choose where to rest and ask your vet early about severe noise fears.
caution: Never force a frightened dog outside or punish fear responses.

title: Safe travel in a car
steps: Use a properly secured crate or suitable dog restraint and plan regular breaks.
Carry water and never leave a dog alone in a parked car in warm conditions.
caution: A car can overheat rapidly even when the outside temperature seems mild.

title: Helping an older dog stay comfortable
steps: Provide supportive bedding, non-slip surfaces and easy access to food and water.
Adjust exercise and discuss stiffness, sleep changes or accidents with your vet.
caution: Do not assume pain or confusion is simply normal ageing.

title: Watching for changes in appetite and mobility
steps: Note changes in eating, drinking, climbing stairs, getting up and willingness to walk.
Arrange a veterinary check for persistent or sudden changes.
caution: Never give human painkillers to dogs unless specifically prescribed.

title: Adapting enrichment for senior dogs
steps: Offer gentle sniffing games and easy food puzzles suited to mobility and senses.
Keep activities short, comfortable and rewarding.
caution: Stop any activity that causes pain, fatigue or distress.

title: Dog-proofing the house
steps: Secure medicines, batteries, chemicals, wires and small objects that could be swallowed.
Check plants and food storage for pet safety and provide safe resting areas.
caution: Contact a vet promptly after suspected ingestion of hazardous items.

title: Safe garden and outdoor spaces
steps: Inspect fences, gates, ponds, sharp tools and garden chemicals.
Supervise access to potentially hazardous plants and compost.
caution: Some fertilisers, slug pellets and plants can be toxic to dogs.

title: Children and dogs together
steps: Supervise all interactions and teach children to respect resting and eating dogs.
Give the dog a quiet retreat that children do not enter.
caution: Never leave young children unsupervised with a dog, even a familiar one.

title: Preparing for a lost dog
steps: Keep microchip contact details current and have a recent clear photo.
If missing, contact local services, chip database and relevant lost-pet organisations.
caution: Do not post sensitive personal information publicly.

title: Emergency planning for pet owners
steps: Keep your vet and out-of-hours numbers, medication list and carrier or lead accessible.
Prepare a small supply of food, water and essential items for unexpected travel.
caution: Seek professional veterinary help for emergencies, not home treatment.
